extracted.intended_audience: The people of the State of New York / general American electorate (readers of the Independent Journal)
extracted.subtask_description: A series of political essays (Federalist Nos. IV–VII) arguing that a single, energetic national government best secures the people's safety by reducing causes of war, improving defense, preventing interstate dissensions, and managing foreign relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimizing just causes of war
rubrics_metrics.description: So far, therefore, as either designed or accidental violations of treaties and the laws of nations afford JUST causes of war, they are less to be apprehended under one general government than under several lesser ones, and in that respect the former most favors the SAFETY of the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A national government, not being affected by local circumstances, is less likely to commit treaty or law violations or to fail to prevent or punish them. Evaluate a government by whether it reduces both designed and accidental violations that constitute just causes of war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection against direct unlawful violence
rubrics_metrics.description: One good national government affords vastly more security against dangers from direct and unlawful violence than can be derived from any other quarter, because such violences are more frequently caused by the passions and interests of a part than of the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a government structure centralizes authority and impartial enforcement so that local passions or partial interests cannot more easily provoke hostilities (examples: Indian hostilities provoked by individual states vs none by the federal government).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity to accommodate and settle disputes amicably
rubrics_metrics.description: But not only fewer just causes of war will be given by the national government, but it will also be more in their power to accommodate and settle them amicably. They will be more temperate and cool ... and will proceed with moderation and candor to consider and decide on the means most proper to extricate them from the difficulties which threaten them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge a government by its ability to negotiate, acknowledge errors, offer explanations and compensations, and obtain peaceful settlements—qualities contrasted with proud, defensive state governments. Example provided: a strong nation obtains acceptable compensation where a small state would not.

rubrics_metrics.name: International dignity and bargaining power
rubrics_metrics.description: Besides, it is well known that acknowledgments, explanations, and compensations are often accepted as satisfactory from a strong united nation, which would be rejected as unsatisfactory if offered by a State or confederacy of little consideration or power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the polity presents a unified, respectable face abroad so that foreign powers are less likely to insult or demand humiliating concessions (example: Genoa forced to send its Doge to France).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding policies that INVITE hostility or insult
rubrics_metrics.description: The safety of the people of America against dangers from FOREIGN force depends not only on their forbearing to give JUST causes of war to other nations, but also on their placing and continuing themselves in such a situation as not to INVITE hostility or insult; for it need not be observed that there are PRETENDED as well as just causes of war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure a government's prudence by whether it organizes itself and its external behavior so as not to provide pretexts (real or pretended) for foreign aggression—includes economic positioning (fisheries, navigation, trade) that may provoke jealousy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Providing the best possible state of defense (unity of resources)
rubrics_metrics.description: That situation consists in the best possible state of defense, and necessarily depends on the government, the arms, and the resources of the country. One government can collect and avail itself of the talents and experience of the ablest men ... It can apply the resources and power of the whole to the defense of any particular part ... more easily and expeditiously than State governments or separate confederacies can possibly do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a polity can marshal national talents, finances, and materials uniformly and rapidly for defense; evaluate central coordination of militias, fleets, and armies versus fragmented efforts (British navy example, hypothetical divided British polities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform military organization and command (militia consolidation)
rubrics_metrics.description: It can place the militia under one plan of discipline, and, by putting their officers in a proper line of subordination to the Chief Magistrate, will, as it were, consolidate them into one corps, and thereby render them more efficient than if divided into thirteen or into three or four distinct independent companies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge governmental design by its ability to create unified command structures, consistent discipline and rapid deployment—contrast the inefficiency and coordination problems of multiple independent militias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding fragmentation that breeds jealousy and unequal power
rubrics_metrics.description: The most sanguine advocates for three or four confederacies cannot reasonably suppose that they would long remain exactly on an equal footing in point of strength ... what human contrivance can secure the continuance of such equality? ... Distrust naturally creates distrust, and by nothing is good-will and kind conduct more speedily changed than by invidious jealousies and uncandid imputations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate proposals for dividing a polity by their tendency to create unequal powers, envy, and rivalry; consider historical evidence that neighboring, unequal states tend toward competition and conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preventing conflicting foreign alliances and commercial interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Each of them would have its commerce with foreigners to regulate by distinct treaties ... Different commercial concerns must create different interests, and of course different degrees of political attachment to and connection with different foreign nations. Hence it might and probably would happen that the foreign nation with whom the SOUTHERN confederacy might be at war would be the one with whom the NORTHERN confederacy would be the most desirous of preserving peace and friendship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a government structure prevents separate parts from crafting divergent foreign policies and treaties that could be exploited by external powers to play them off against each other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical remedies against neighborhood-induced hostility
rubrics_metrics.description: So far is the general sense of mankind from corresponding with the tenets of those who endeavor to lull asleep our apprehensions of discord and hostility between the States ... that it has from long observation of the progress of society become a sort of axiom in politics, that vicinity or nearness of situation, constitutes nations natural enemies ... This passage, at the same time, points out the EVIL and suggests the REMEDY.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating constitutional arrangements, consider the axiom that neighboring polities commonly become hostile unless constitutional structures (i.e., confederate republic with preventing provisions or a union) mitigate neighborhood jealousies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preventing internecine causes of war (territorial disputes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Territorial disputes have at all times been found one of the most fertile sources of hostility among nations. ... A dismemberment of the Confederacy, however, would revive this dispute, and would create others on the same subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the government provides an impartial umpire or mechanism for adjudicating rival territorial claims (example: western unsettled lands, cessions to the Union). Absence of such mechanisms makes hostility over territory more likely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding coordination problems in allied defense and diplomacy
rubrics_metrics.description: How, and when, and in what proportion shall aids of men and money be afforded? Who shall command the allied armies, and from which of them shall he receive his orders? Who shall settle the terms of peace, and in case of disputes what umpire shall decide between them and compel acquiescence? Various difficulties and inconveniences would be inseparable from such a situation; whereas one government ... would be free from all these embarrassments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess systems for their ability to answer practical questions of coalition defense and post-conflict settlement; fragmentation creates irresolvable administrative and command questions that a single government avoids.
